questions.q: What is the key difference between a baseline and a control condition, per this lesson?
options: A baseline requires shots; a control does not
A baseline is the reference point a result is measured against; a control is an experimental run designed specifically to isolate whether your intended variable caused the effect
They are exactly the same thing with two different names
A control is always run on a simulator, while a baseline is always run on real hardware
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes them explicitly: a baseline is a reference value/condition, while a control is designed to rule out confounds so you can trust that your intended variable, not something else, produced the observed effect.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say comparing your result against a baseline number from someone else's paper, published months earlier on possibly different hardware, is not a controlled comparison?
options: Because baselines from other papers are always fabricated
Because published papers are never allowed to be used as baselines
Because too many things differ besides the one variable being tested -- hardware, calibration window, and time all differ at once
Because quantum hardware never changes over time, so this concern doesn't actually apply
questions.explain: The lesson explains that real quantum hardware drifts over time due to recalibration and usage, so a comparison across different hardware, time, and calibration windows confounds multiple variables at once -- it is not a controlled comparison.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend interleaving control and treatment runs in time, rather than running all controls first and all treatments hours later?
options: Because interleaving runs faster on quantum hardware
To average out hardware drift across both groups instead of letting drift become a confound for only one group
Because quantum hardware requires alternating job types by policy
Because interleaving eliminates the need for multiple shots
questions.explain: The lesson states interleaving control and treatment runs specifically averages out hardware drift across both groups rather than letting one group absorb more of the drift than the other.

questions.q: Why is reporting a quantum circuit result from a single shot described as unreliable?
options: A single shot always returns a classical bit string with zero error, making it trivially unreliable
Single shots are always technically impossible to execute on real hardware
Shots have nothing to do with measurement in quantum computing
A single shot is one probabilistic projective measurement, like judging a coin's fairness from one flip, rather than a measured probability distribution
questions.explain: The lesson compares a single shot to judging a coin's fairness from one flip -- quantum measurement is inherently probabilistic, so many shots are needed to build a probability distribution with quantifiable statistical uncertainty.

questions.q: Why can't a noiseless simulator and real noisy hardware be treated as interchangeable baselines for a hypothesis about an error-mitigation technique?
options: A noiseless simulator has no noise to mitigate, so it can't test a mitigation technique's effect at all
Mitigation techniques only work on simulators, never on real hardware
Simulators and hardware always produce identical results, so the choice doesn't matter
Real hardware is always faster than a simulator, making comparison invalid
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a noise-mitigation hypothesis tested only on a noiseless simulator tells you nothing, since there is no noise present for the technique to mitigate -- the choice of simulator vs. hardware is itself a design decision tied to what the hypothesis actually claims.
